title: Route Farthest From the Thieves
statement:
You get an n × n grid. grid[r][c] = 1 means a thief stands in that cell, and 0 means it is empty. There is at least one thief.

You walk from the top-left cell (0, 0) to the bottom-right cell (n − 1, n − 1), moving up, down, left or right. You may step on any cell, thieves included.

The safety of a route is the smallest Manhattan distance |r1 − r2| + |c1 − c2| between any cell on the route (start and end included) and any thief. Return the largest safety any route can have.

examples.why: Going down the left column and along the bottom row keeps every cell at least 2 from the thief. The start and the end are exactly 2 away, so nothing beats 2.
The start cell holds a thief, so every route has safety 0.
The left column passes next to the thief (distance 1). Going right along the top and down the right side keeps every cell at least 2 away. The start's only neighbours are 2 away, so 3 is impossible.

hints: First answer a simpler question for every cell: how far is the nearest thief? Running a separate search from each thief is too slow.
Start one BFS from all thieves at once. Then ask: is there a route using only cells at distance ≥ d? That check is a plain BFS, and it is monotonic in d.
Binary search on d, or skip it: always expand the reachable cell with the largest distance first (a max-heap). The smallest distance you had to accept on the way to the end is the answer.

explain.intuition:
Two separate problems hide here. The first is "distance from every cell to the nearest thief". Put all thieves into the BFS queue at distance 0 and expand together; each cell is reached first by its nearest thief. That is one O(n²) pass instead of one pass per thief.

The second is a "widest path": maximise the smallest value along a route. If you can stay at distance ≥ d, you can also stay at ≥ d − 1, so you can binary search on d with a flood-fill check. Or run a Dijkstra-like search with a max-heap: always step into the safest reachable cell next. The route's safety is the minimum distance popped before reaching the end. It is the same idea as finding the strongest chain in a network, where a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
steps: Multi-source BFS from every thief to fill dist[r][c], the distance to the nearest thief.
Push (dist[0][0], 0, 0) into a max-heap and mark it seen. Keep safety = dist[0][0].
Pop the cell with the largest distance and lower safety to it if needed. If it is the bottom-right cell, return safety.
Push every unseen neighbour with its distance, mark it seen, and repeat.
pitfalls: Running a BFS from each thief separately. With many thieves that is O(n⁴).
Using Euclidean distance or counting steps through the route instead of the plain Manhattan distance to the nearest thief.
Forgetting that the start and end cells count. If either holds a thief, the answer is 0.

solutions.title: Multi-source BFS + binary search on the safety
solutions.idea: Compute every cell's distance to the nearest thief, then binary search the largest d for which cells with distance ≥ d connect start to end.

solutions.title: Multi-source BFS + max-heap walk
solutions.idea: After the distance BFS, always expand the safest reachable cell next. The lowest distance accepted before reaching the end is the answer.

followups: Solve the second part with union-find: add cells from the safest down and stop when start and end join.
Thieves move one step per minute. How would you model the grid then?
